summary: Describes TSIG, a way to authenticate DNS transactions using a shared secret and a one-way hash. It can verify that dynamic updates to a zone come from an approved client, or that responses come from an approved name server. How the secrets are distributed is left to the network administrator.

eli5.summary: Two computers share a secret password. Each stamps its messages with a seal made from that password, so the other can tell the message is genuine and untampered.

questions: how to authenticate dns updates with a shared secret
how does tsig authenticate dns messages
what is the tsig fudge value
subtitle: Authenticate DNS requests and responses with a shared secret and a keyed hash, appended as a TSIG record.

tldr.problem: DNS transactions such as dynamic updates and zone transfers need a cheap way to confirm that a message came from an approved party and was not altered, without the cost of public key signatures.
tldr.mechanism: Two parties agree on a key and algorithm in advance. The sender computes a keyed hash (MAC) over the DNS message and some TSIG variables and puts it in a TSIG record at the end of the additional section; the receiver recomputes and compares it.
tldr.outcome: This revision obsoletes RFC 2845 and RFC 4635 and fixes a check-ordering problem that let implementations sign replies with an unvalidated request MAC. The wire format is unchanged.

today: RFC 8945 is an Internet Standard. It obsoletes RFC 2845 and RFC 4635, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What TSIG Is For
sections.content:
TSIG (Secret Key Transaction Authentication) gives point-to-point authentication and integrity checking for DNS transactions using a message authentication code (MAC) made from a keyed hash. Uses include DNS update requests and responses, as a lightweight alternative to the public key approach of RFC 3007, and protecting zone transfers, including glue records that DNSSEC does not protect.

Both parties must agree on an algorithm and key beforehand. How they agree is out of scope, and the RFC expects an administrator to configure name servers and clients out of band. The shared keys must be protected like private keys.

The RFC says the scheme is unsuitable for general server-to-server authentication or for servers that talk to many others, because the number of shared keys grows quadratically. It does suit resolvers on hosts that only talk to a few recursive servers.
sections.eli5: Two computers agree on a secret ahead of time. It works well for a few pairs of friends, but would be a mess if everyone had to share a separate secret with everyone else.

sections.title: The TSIG Record
sections.content:
TSIG is a meta-RR with type code 250. It is computed for one transaction, MUST NOT be cached, and is discarded after it has authenticated a message. The record's NAME is the key name, TYPE is TSIG, CLASS MUST be ANY and TTL MUST be 0.

The RDATA fields are: Algorithm Name (not compressed), a 48-bit Time Signed in seconds since 1970-01-01 UTC, a 16-bit Fudge giving the allowed time difference in seconds, MAC Size and MAC, the Original ID of the request, an Error code (zero in requests), and Other Len with Other Data. Other Data is empty except for a BADTIME error, where it holds the server's current time.

The RFC defines four error codes that may appear in the Error field: 16 (BADSIG), 17 (BADKEY), 18 (BADTIME) and 22 (BADTRUNC).
sections.eli5: The TSIG record is the stamp on the letter. It says which secret was used, when it was stamped, and carries the stamp pattern itself.

sections.title: How the MAC Is Computed
sections.content:
The inputs are fed to the hash as one continuous octet sequence in network byte order or wire format, with no separators or padding. For a request the digest covers the DNS message and the TSIG variables. For a response it covers the request MAC, the response message and the TSIG variables.

When signing, the message is taken before the TSIG RR is added and before ARCOUNT is incremented. When verifying, the TSIG RR is removed, ARCOUNT is decremented, and the message ID is replaced with the Original ID if they differ, for example when a dynamic update is forwarded.

The TSIG variables are the key name, CLASS, TTL, Algorithm Name, Time Signed, Fudge, Error, Other Len and Other Data. Including the two timers defends against replay: otherwise an attacker could replay an old message with fresh Time Signed and Fudge values.
sections.eli5: The stamp is made by mixing the whole letter with the secret and a timestamp. Change any part of the letter or the time and the stamp stops matching.

sections.title: Request and Response Processing
sections.content:
A client signs a request and appends a single TSIG RR as the last record of the additional section. It MUST remember the MAC and key name while it waits for the answer. A server that receives a message with more than one TSIG, or one in the wrong position, drops it and returns FORMERR.

The server MUST then check, in this order: the key, the MAC, the time values and the truncation policy. An unknown key gives RCODE 9 (NOTAUTH) with BADKEY, and a bad MAC gives NOTAUTH with BADSIG. Both responses MUST be unsigned. If the server time is outside Time Signed plus or minus Fudge, it returns BADTIME and signs that response with the client's key, including its own time in Other Data. A MAC that is too short for local policy gives BADTRUNC.

Clients that get an unsigned or unverifiable answer SHOULD NOT accept it, and should log the error and keep waiting for a signed response until the request times out. A forwarding server that does not share the key named in a TSIG forwards the message unchanged.

For TCP sessions with several messages, such as zone transfers, every message in the response must carry a TSIG. A client MUST accept up to 99 intermediary messages without one, and MUST verify that the first and last message have one. If verification fails the client MUST close the connection.
sections.eli5: The receiver checks the stamp in a fixed order: is this a secret I know, does the stamp match, is the time right. If something is wrong, it sends back an unstamped note rather than a stamped one.

sections.title: Algorithms and MAC Truncation
sections.content:
Implementations that support TSIG MUST implement HMAC SHA1 and HMAC SHA256. The RFC recommends hmac-sha256 and marks hmac-sha1 as NOT RECOMMENDED for use, and existing uses SHOULD be replaced with hmac-sha256 or another SHA-2 algorithm. HMAC-MD5 implementation is optional and its use is MUST NOT. Others such as gss-tsig and hmac-sha384 are MAY.

A MAC may be truncated by keeping its leading octets. A MAC Size greater than the hash output, or smaller than the larger of 10 octets and half the hash length, MUST cause the message to be dropped with FORMERR (the zero-size error responses are the exception). Local policy decides the shortest acceptable MAC, and a reply SHOULD use a MAC at least as long as the one in the request.

The RFC also says the secret SHOULD be at least as long as the keyed hash output.
sections.eli5: There is a menu of recipes for making the stamp. The RFC says to pick the stronger ones and stay away from the old weak one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
TSIG is much cheaper than DNSSEC signatures and gives strong authentication between two systems as long as the shared key is not compromised. Secrets SHOULD NOT be shared by more than two entities, because any holder could impersonate another. There SHOULD be only one algorithm per key name to prevent cross-algorithm attacks.

TSIG authenticates the transmission between two parties, not the original data. The Fudge value is a trade-off: too large may allow replay attacks and too small may cause failures from clock skew or delays. The RECOMMENDED value in most situations is 300 seconds.

The RFC fixes a problem in RFC 2845. That RFC checked the time values before the request MAC, so an implementation could fail to run further checks and use an invalid request MAC in a signed reply. Now the request MAC is treated as invalid until validated, so any answer must be unsigned until then, and the MAC is checked before the time values.
sections.eli5: The old rules let a receiver stamp its reply using a request stamp it had not yet checked. The fix is simple: check the stamp first, then reply.

sections.title: Why This Revision Exists
sections.content:
TSIG was first specified in RFC 2845. In 2017, two name server implementations that followed that document and RFC 4635 strictly were found to have security problems tied to the feature, which were tracked as three CVEs. They were fixed, and to avoid similar problems the two RFCs were updated and merged into this one.

The RFC says that there are no changes in interoperability. TSIG on the wire is still the same mechanism, and only the checking semantics changed.
sections.eli5: Some programs followed the old rules too literally and had a bug. The rules were tidied up so the bug cannot happen again, and the stamp looks the same as before.
